To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) AMS data from two UK cities were analysed using PMF, (b) three POA factors were identified, (c) the mass emission ratios of the combustion aerosol factors were derived and compared with other studies, (d) the mass spectra of the POA factors were compared with those from other studies, and (e) the mass spectra were matched with emissions from laboratory experiments.
PMF was applied to organic AMS data from three UK cities, and three primary organic sources were identified, with mass emission ratios of POA relative to CO derived for two of these.
PMF applied to AMS data can be used to identify sources of primary organic matter in urban aerosols.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantification of primary organic aerosols and their sources, using a novel approach.
the quantification of the contributions of primary organic aerosols from traffic, cooking and solid-fuel combustion to ambient particulate matter in two UK cities, London and Manchester.

the application of PMF analysis to AMS data and has provided the first estimates of the contributions of traffic, cooking and biomass burning to the POA fraction of fine particles in two UK cities, which are of a similar magnitude to those previously reported for other locations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PMF approach can be used to provide a consistent and robust source attribution for organic aerosols in urban environments.
the AMS can be applied to urban organic aerosol measurements and that the data can be used to identify and quantify sources of primary organic particulate matter.
cooking and traffic emissions represent 40-60% and 10-30% of primary organic aerosols during the winter, respectively, in the UK.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cooking and solid fuel aerosols represent a significant fraction of POA in the UK, particularly in winter and in the absence of strong photochemical activity.
cooking aerosols are likely to represent the largest source of POA in the UK, followed by traffic, and that biomass burning may be an important source in some locations, but not others.
the AMS has proved to be a valuable source apportionment tool in the context of organic aerosols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PMF can be used to identify and quantify the sources of primary organic matter in urban aerosol.
PMF analysis of AMS data is a robust approach for identifying and quantifying sources of POA.
PMF is a useful technique for source attribution and profiling in AMS data, but it is not a silver bullet.
